We evaluate our method on three image captioning benchmarks using five different LVLMs, demonstrating its effectiveness in significantly reducing hallucinations. Further experiments reveal a trade-off between reduced hallucinations and richer details. Notably, our method allows for manual adjustment of the model's conservativeness, enabling flexible control to meet diverse real-world requirements.

papers.title: Why Can't Transformers Learn Multiplication? Reverse-Engineering Reveals Long-Range Dependency Pitfalls
papers.research_question: Why do transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication?
papers.core_contribution: By reverse-engineering a successful implicit chain-of-thought model, the paper uncovers that transformers fail at multiplication due to a lack of long-range dependencies, and demonstrates that an auxiliary loss providing the correct inductive bias can enable learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication due to a pitfall in learning long-range dependencies with gradient descent and an auto-regressive loss, but this can be addressed with the correct inductive bias, as demonstrated by the auxiliary loss method.
papers.key_findings:
The ICoT model learns the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication, while standard fine-tuning does not.
The ICoT model encodes long-range dependencies via attention patterns that form a directed acyclic graph (attention tree) to cache and retrieve pairwise partial products.
The ICoT model implements partial products in attention heads as Minkowski sums and represents digits using a Fourier basis, forming an efficient pentagonal prism structure.
Standard fine-tuning converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies, causing loss to plateau on middle digits.
An auxiliary loss that supervises the prediction of a 'running partial sum' via a linear regression probe provides an inductive bias that enables the model to learn multiplication successfully.
papers.limitation: The suggested inductive bias is task-specific and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Developing generalizing inductive biases for tasks with long-range dependencies.
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly capable, yet still fail at a seemingly simple task of multi-digit multiplication. In this work, we study why, by reverse-engineering a model that successfully learns multiplication via \emph{implicit chain-of-thought}, and report three findings: (1) Evidence of long-range structure: Logit attributions and linear probes indicate that the model encodes the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication. (2) Mechanism: the model encodes long-range dependencies using attention to construct a directed acyclic graph to ``cache'' and ``retrieve'' pairwise partial products. (3) Geometry: the model implements partial products in attention heads by forming Minkowski sums between pairs of digits, and digits are represented using a Fourier basis, both of which are intuitive and efficient representations that the standard fine-tuning model lacks. With these insights, we revisit the learning dynamics of standard fine-tuning and find that the model converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies. We further validate this understanding by introducing an auxiliary loss that predicts the ``running sum'' via a linear regression probe, which provides an inductive bias that enables the model to successfully learn multi-digit multiplication. In summary, by reverse-engineering the mechanisms of an implicit chain-of-thought model we uncover a pitfall for learning long-range dependencies in Transformers and provide an example of how the correct inductive bias can address this issue.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Patches of Nonlinearity: Instruction Vectors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do instruction-tuned language models internally process instructions, specifically how are instruction-specific representations constructed and utilized during post-training (SFT and DPO)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that instruction vectors (IVs) are localized, superadditive representations that act as circuit selectors, and introduces a novel method to analyze information flow without linear assumptions.
papers.conclusion: Instruction vectors are formed eagerly and act as circuit selectors, with their superadditive nature challenging existing linear assumptions in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Instruction vectors (IVs) are localized in the residual stream at the final instructional token.
IVs exhibit superadditivity: their combined causal influence is greater than the sum of individual influences.
IVs are linearly separable in representation space but interact non-linearly.
IVs act as circuit selectors, conditioning on task representations to select different information pathways in later layers.
Instruction tuning is necessary for IVs to acquire circuit-selection ability.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of instruction-tuned language models and their ubiquitous usage, very little is known of how models process instructions internally. In this work, we address this gap from a mechanistic point of view by investigating how instruction-specific representations are constructed and utilized in different stages of post-training: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Via causal mediation, we identify that instruction representation is fairly localized in models. These representations, which we call Instruction Vectors (IVs), demonstrate a curious juxtaposition of linear separability along with non-linear causal interaction, broadly questioning the scope of the linear representation hypothesis commonplace in mechanistic interpretability. To disentangle the non-linear causal interaction, we propose a novel method to localize information processing in language models that is free from the implicit linear assumptions of patching-based techniques. We find that, conditioned on the task representations formed in the early layers, different information pathways are selected in the later layers to solve that task, i.e., IVs act as circuit selectors.

papers.title: Towards Visual Explanations for Convolutional Neural Networks via Input Resampling
papers.research_question: How can we explain convolutional neural network predictions by analyzing internal neuron activations and their correlation with outputs over perturbed inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework to explain CNN predictions by selecting important neurons based on activation-output correlation and activation precision metrics over perturbed inputs, and visualizing their corresponding image patches via deconvolution.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework analyzes CNN predictions by selecting neurons with high correlation to output and precise activations, suggesting ways to incorporate such metrics into training for improved efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Activation precision metric selects neurons that activate on generalizable features, enabling a secondary classifier trained on patches to outperform the full network early in training.
Activation-output correlation metric selects neurons that exert large influence over the network output.
The sets of neurons selected by the two metrics converge as network accuracy improves, indicating alignment between influential and generalizable features.
The framework can be used for weakly supervised localization, identifying image patches that contain the object of interest.
Patches selected by activation precision achieve higher localization accuracy compared to baseline metrics.
future_direction: Incorporating the proposed metrics into neural network training to improve training efficiency.
papers.abstract: The predictive power of neural networks often costs model interpretability. Several techniques have been developed for explaining model outputs in terms of input features; however, it is difficult to translate such interpretations into actionable insight. Here, we propose a framework to analyze predictions in terms of the model's internal features by inspecting information flow through the network. Given a trained network and a test image, we select neurons by two metrics, both measured over a set of images created by perturbations to the input image: (1) magnitude of the correlation between the neuron activation and the network output and (2) precision of the neuron activation. We show that the former metric selects neurons that exert large influence over the network output while the latter metric selects neurons that activate on generalizable features. By comparing the sets of neurons selected by these two metrics, our framework suggests a way to investigate the internal attention mechanisms of convolutional neural networks.

papers.title: Switching between internal and external modes: A multiscale learning principle
papers.research_question: How are internal models learned in neural systems? The paper proposes that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that switching between internally and externally biased modes of processing at multiple timescales generates an error signal that drives learning in neural systems, enabling the construction and refinement of internal models.
papers.conclusion: Switching between internal and external modes is a multiscale learning principle that allows neural circuits to generate error signals for updating internal models, with predictions that disruption of switching impairs learning and integration of new information.
papers.key_findings:
Mode-switching occurs in diverse neural systems (e.g., hippocampus, neocortex) across timescales from milliseconds to hours.
In the hippocampus, alternating phases of theta oscillations separate encoding (external mode) and retrieval (internal mode) and are linked to synaptic plasticity.
In the neocortex, oscillations like alpha rhythms reflect shifts between feedforward (external) and feedback (internal) processing, influencing perception and learning.
Whole-brain states such as awake rest, default mode network activity, and sleep (non-REM/REM cycles) represent large-scale internal/external mode switches that benefit memory consolidation and integration.
Cholinergic modulation is a common mechanism that biases processing toward external modes across multiple systems.
future_direction: Test the prediction that disruption of mode-switching (e.g., between non-REM and REM sleep) impairs integration of new hippocampal memories with existing neocortical knowledge.
Investigate how altering the timescale of switching affects the learning of temporally extended features.
Explore the role of neuromodulators like acetylcholine in regulating mode-switching and learning across different brain systems.
papers.abstract: Brains construct internal models that support perception, prediction, and action in the external world. Individual circuits within a brain also learn internal models of the local world of input they receive, in order to facilitate efficient and robust representation. How are these internal models learned? We propose that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing. We review computational evidence that this mode-switching can produce an error signal to drive learning. We then consider empirical evidence for the instantiation of mode-switching in diverse neural systems, ranging from subsecond fluctuations in the hippocampus to wake-sleep alternations across the whole brain. We hypothesize that these internal/external switching processes, which occur at multiple scales, can drive learning at each scale. This framework predicts that (a) slower mode-switching should be associated with learning of more temporally extended input features and (b) disruption of switching should impair the integration of new information with prior information.

papers.title: Explainable Reinforcement Learning via Interpretable Policy Distillation
papers.research_question: How to provide human-understandable explanations for deep reinforcement learning policies via interpretable policy distillation while maintaining high fidelity and performance?
papers.core_contribution: A unified framework for explainable reinforcement learning via interpretable policy distillation that achieves high fidelity, competitive performance, and both global and local explanations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework enables trustworthy deployment of RL agents in safety-critical applications by providing interpretable policies with high fidelity and performance.
papers.key_findings:
Distilled interpretable policies achieve high fidelity with minimal performance loss compared to teacher deep RL policies.
Ablation studies show that tree depth, loss function, and dataset size significantly impact fidelity and transparency.
Decision trees provide global explanations via the full tree structure and local explanations via path tracing for specific states.
papers.limitation:
Scaling to high-dimensional and visual inputs
Continuous control requires extensions of trees or sparse models
Online or incremental distillation for data efficiency
Human evaluation of explanations
Robustness under distribution shifts or rare states
Exploring interpretable frameworks beyond trees and linear policies
future_direction: Scaling to high-dimensional and visual inputs
Continuous control extensions
Online or incremental distillation for data efficiency
papers.abstract: Abstract—Deep reinforcement learning achieves remarkable performance but often operates as a black box, limiting trust in safety-critical applications. Explainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL) aims to provide human-understandable explanations. We propose a unified framework for XRL via interpretable policy distillation, where a high-performing teacher policy is distilled into interpretable models such as decision trees or sparse linear policies. The distilled policy enables both global and local expla- nations while maintaining high fidelity. We provide theoretical guarantees on fidelity and performance, and perform extensive experiments with ablation studies. Results show that interpretable policies achieve competitive performance with high transparency, enabling deployment in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Revealing the Dark Secrets of BERT
papers.research_question: What are the common attention patterns in BERT, how do they change during fine-tuning, and how important are individual heads for task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's attention heads exhibit redundant patterns, indicating overparametrization, and that selectively disabling heads can improve performance on GLUE tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that BERT can benefit from disabling attention heads due to redundancy in encoded information, and suggests model pruning as a future direction.
papers.key_findings:
Five common attention patterns (vertical, diagonal, vertical+diagonal, block, heterogeneous) are repeated across heads, with only the heterogeneous pattern potentially capturing linguistically meaningful information.
Two heads in pre-trained BERT show attention patterns correlated with FrameNet semantic relations, but these heads are not important for GLUE task performance.
Fine-tuning changes attention patterns primarily in the last two layers of BERT.
Disabling certain attention heads can improve performance on GLUE tasks, with gains of up to 3.2% absolute improvement.
BERT is overparametrized, with redundant information encoded across heads.
future_direction: Study self-attention patterns in different languages, especially verb-final and free-word-order languages.
Investigate model pruning and finding optimal sub-architectures to reduce redundancy.
papers.abstract: Olga Kovaleva, Alexey Romanov, Anna Rogers, Anna Rumshisky. Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (EMNLP-IJCNLP). 2019.

papers.title: Training-Trajectory-Aware Token Selection
papers.research_question: What goes wrong during continual reasoning distillation? The paper investigates why naive continual distillation often fails in the frontier regime, characterized by a performance drop (Imitation Shock) despite decreasing loss, and how to overcome it.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Imitation Shock, a performance bottleneck in continual distillation caused by imitation-anchor tokens, and proposes T3S, a token-selection method that masks these anchors to clear the optimization path for yet-to-learn tokens, improving distillation efficiency and performance.
papers.conclusion: T3S effectively addresses the limitations of continual distillation by using training-trajectory signals to select and mask imitation-anchor tokens, leading to state-of-the-art performance on reasoning benchmarks with minimal data.
papers.key_findings:
Imitation Shock is a universal phenomenon in continual distillation where performance drops sharply then recovers, despite monotonic loss decrease.
Pre-bottleneck updates are harmful; discarding them (Recovering Residual Transfer) yields better performance than standard distillation.
Token-level analysis reveals imitation-anchor tokens that dominate early optimization and suppress the learning of other tokens.
T3S, which masks imitation-anchor tokens, consistently improves distillation performance for both autoregressive and diffusion language models.
T3S also reduces inference cost (fewer generated tokens) for diffusion language models.
papers.limitation:
T3S requires monitoring training accuracy to identify the imitation bottleneck, which assumes access to gold answers or a verifier.
The method is evaluated primarily on math and code reasoning; broader domains remain to be tested.
future_direction: Extend T3S to broader domains beyond math and code reasoning.
Explore cross-model token selection, using a small selector model for a larger tokenizer-sharing model.
Scale the method to larger models and more diverse distillation settings.
papers.abstract: Efficient distillation is a key pathway for converting expensive reasoning capability into deployable efficiency, yet in the frontier regime where the student already has strong reasoning ability, naive continual distillation often yields limited gains or even degradation. We observe a characteristic training phenomenon: even as loss decreases monotonically, all performance metrics can drop sharply at almost the same bottleneck, before gradually recovering. We further uncover a token-level mechanism: confidence bifurcates into steadily increasing Imitation-Anchor Tokens that quickly anchor optimization and other yet-to-learn tokens whose confidence is suppressed until after the bottleneck. And the characteristic that these two types of tokens cannot coexist is the root cause of the failure in continual distillation. To this end, we propose Training-Trajectory-Aware Token Selection (T3S) to reconstruct the training objective at the token level, clearing the optimization path for yet-to-learn tokens. T3 yields consistent gains in both AR and dLLM settings: with only hundreds of examples, Qwen3-8B surpasses DeepSeek-R1 on competitive reasoning benchmarks, Qwen3-32B approaches Qwen3-235B, and T3-trained LLaDA-2.0-Mini exceeds its AR baseline, achieving state-of-the-art performance among all of 16B-scale no-think models.

papers.title: From Associations to Activations: Comparing Behavioral and Hidden-State Semantic Geometry in LLMs
papers.research_question: To what extent can an LLM's hidden-state geometry be recovered from its behavior in psycholinguistic experiments?
papers.core_contribution: Forced-choice behavioral similarity aligns more with hidden-state geometry than free association, and behavioral similarity (especially forced choice) predicts hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines and cross-model consensus, indicating that behavior-only measurements retain recoverable information about internal semantic geometry.
papers.conclusion: Large-scale behavioral probing recovers meaningful structure in hidden-state semantic geometry, but fidelity depends on the measurement channel; forced-choice behavior provides substantially stronger and more reliable alignment than free association, which is too noisy to add much signal beyond shared cross-model structure.
papers.key_findings:
Forced-choice behavior aligns substantially more with hidden-state geometry than free association.
Alignment is stronger when hidden states are extracted under task-aligned prompts (e.g., using the same prompt as the behavioral task).
Behavioral similarity, especially from forced choice, predicts unseen hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines (FastText, BERT) and cross-model consensus.
Cross-model consensus shows high alignment with hidden states, indicating a shared semantic geometry across diverse LLMs.
Free association is noisier and adds little signal beyond shared cross-model structure.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to nouns and English.
The vocabulary size is 5,000 words, which may not capture full semantic space.
Only instruction-tuned decoder models are analyzed, limiting generalizability.
The analysis is correlational, not causal; alignment claims would be stronger with causal tests.
Scaling to larger models and different architectures is unclear.
future_direction: Expand beyond nouns and English to other word classes and languages.
Conduct causal tests by modifying internal activations to see if behavioral similarity shifts accordingly.
Assess generality by expanding to more models and architectures.
papers.abstract: We investigate the extent to which an LLM's hidden-state geometry can be recovered from its behavior in psycholinguistic experiments. Across eight instruction-tuned transformer models, we run two experimental paradigms -- similarity-based forced choice and free association -- over a shared 5,000-word vocabulary, collecting 17.5M+ trials to build behavior-based similarity matrices. Using representational similarity analysis, we compare behavioral geometries to layerwise hidden-state similarity and benchmark against FastText, BERT, and cross-model consensus. We find that forced-choice behavior aligns substantially more with hidden-state geometry than free association. In a held-out-words regression, behavioral similarity (especially forced choice) predicts unseen hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines and cross-model consensus, indicating that behavior-only measurements retain recoverable information about internal semantic geometry. Finally, we discuss implications for the ability of behavioral tasks to uncover hidden cognitive states.

papers.title: When BERT Plays the Lottery, All Tickets Are Winning
papers.research_question: Does the lottery ticket hypothesis hold for fine-tuned BERT, and do the resulting 'good' subnetworks encode meaningful linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The lottery ticket hypothesis holds for fine-tuned BERT, but even the worst subnetworks are trainable, suggesting that most pre-trained weights are useful. The winning tickets are unstable and do not encode clear linguistic patterns.
papers.conclusion: While winning tickets exist in BERT, they are not stable and do not necessarily encode linguistic knowledge. Moreover, most pre-trained BERT weights are useful.
papers.key_findings:
"Good" subnetworks (winning tickets) exist in fine-tuned BERT, achieving ~90% of full model performance.
"Bad" subnetworks (the complement) can also be fine-tuned to achieve reasonable performance, sometimes comparable to BiLSTM baselines.
The "good" subnetworks are unstable across different random initializations during fine-tuning.
The "good" subnetworks do not show a higher proportion of linguistically meaningful attention patterns compared to the full model.
There is considerable interaction between self-attention heads and MLPs; pruning them together is more efficient.
papers.limitation: The subnetworks are identified using the dev set and may not generalize to other data.
future_direction: Further study of the interaction between BERT's self-attention heads and MLPs.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based models were shown to be reducible to a smaller number of self-attention heads and layers. We consider this phenomenon from the perspective of the lottery ticket hypothesis, using both structured and magnitude pruning. For fine-tuned BERT, we show that (a) it is possible to find subnetworks achieving performance that is comparable with that of the full model, and (b) similarly-sized subnetworks sampled from the rest of the model perform worse. Strikingly, with structured pruning even the worst possible subnetworks remain highly trainable, indicating that most pre-trained BERT weights are potentially useful. We also study the "good" subnetworks to see if their success can be attributed to superior linguistic knowledge, but find them unstable, and not explained by meaningful self-attention patterns.

papers.title: Analyzing Vision Transformers for Image Classification in Class Embedding Space
papers.research_question: How do Vision Transformers build categorical representations for image classification, and how do self-attention and MLP layers contribute to this process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to project Vision Transformers' internal representations onto the class embedding space, enabling analysis of how class representations are built and the differential roles of self-attention and MLP layers via key-value memory pair mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework is a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability of Vision Transformers, providing insights into their category-building processes.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens develop class-specific representations from early stages, with class identifiability increasing across blocks.
Attention mechanisms and contextual information are crucial for building class representations; image tokens cannot develop class-identifiable representations in isolation.
Self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute: MLP layers promote strong categorical updates in late blocks, while self-attention layers promote weaker but more disseminated updates earlier.
The framework can identify image regions important for class detection and outperforms linear probing in revealing task-relevant features.
Key-value memory pair mechanisms in MLP and self-attention layers are involved in building class representations, with agreement rates correlating with model accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Only studies Vision Transformers trained for image classification.
Does not explore model editing or performance improvement applications.
future_direction: Adapt the framework to models with other types of output embeddings.
Use the mechanistic insights for model editing or performance improvement.
papers.abstract: Despite the growing use of transformer models in computer vision, a mechanistic understanding of these networks is still needed. This work introduces a method to reverse-engineer Vision Transformers trained to solve image classification tasks. Inspired by previous research in NLP, we demonstrate how the inner representations at any level of the hierarchy can be projected onto the learned class embedding space to uncover how these networks build categorical representations for their predictions. We use our framework to show how image tokens develop class-specific representations that depend on attention mechanisms and contextual information, and give insights on how self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute to this categorical composition. We additionally demonstrate that this method (1) can be used to determine the parts of an image that would be important for detecting the class of interest, and (2) exhibits significant advantages over traditional linear probing approaches. Taken together, our results position our proposed framework as a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability research.

papers.title: Inferring hidden structure in multilayered neural circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reconstruct the response properties of hidden neurons in multilayered neural circuits using cascaded LN-LN models, and what insights does this provide about retinal processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a computational framework using non-smooth regularization and proximal consensus algorithms to fit hierarchical LN-LN models from limited neural data, revealing that retinal ganglion cell computation can be modeled as a boolean OR function of bipolar cell feature detectors and that visual redundancies are removed primarily at bipolar cell synapses.
papers.conclusion: The developed framework efficiently learns hierarchical nonlinear models from limited data, providing insights into retinal computation and offering a general tool for studying sensory processing across diverse modalities.
papers.key_findings:
LN-LN models demonstrate a 53% improvement in predicting ganglion cell spikes over classical LN models.
Internal nonlinear subunits of the model match properties of retinal bipolar cells in both receptive field structure and number.
Subunits have consistently high thresholds, suppressing all but a small fraction of inputs, leading to sparse activity patterns.
The removal of visual redundancies through stimulus decorrelation across space originates primarily from bipolar cell synapses.
The composite nonlinear computation performed by retinal circuitry corresponds to a boolean OR function applied to bipolar cell feature detectors.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in sensory neuroscience involves understanding how neural circuits shape computations across cascaded cell layers. Here we attempt to reconstruct the response properties of experimentally unobserved neurons in the interior of a multilayered neural circuit, using cascaded linear-nonlinear (LN-LN) models. We combine non-smooth regularization with proximal consensus algorithms to overcome difficulties in fitting such models that arise from the high dimensionality of their parameter space. We apply this framework to retinal ganglion cell processing, learning LN-LN models of retinal circuitry consisting of thousands of parameters, using 40 minutes of responses to white noise. Our models demonstrate a 53% improvement in predicting ganglion cell spikes over classical linear-nonlinear (LN) models. Internal nonlinear subunits of the model match properties of retinal bipolar cells in both receptive field structure and number. Subunits have consistently high thresholds, supressing all but a small fraction of inputs, leading to sparse activity patterns in which only one subunit drives ganglion cell spiking at any time. From the model's parameters, we predict that the removal of visual redundancies through stimulus decorrelation across space, a central tenet of efficient coding theory, originates primarily from bipolar cell synapses. Furthermore, the composite nonlinear computation performed by retinal circuitry corresponds to a boolean OR function applied to bipolar cell feature detectors. Our methods are statistically and computationally efficient, enabling us to rapidly learn hierarchical non-linear models as well as efficiently compute widely used descriptive statistics such as the spike triggered average (STA) and covariance (STC) for high dimensional stimuli. This general computational framework may aid in extracting principles of nonlinear hierarchical sensory processing across diverse modalities from limited data.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Leveraging attention to uncover novel relationships or more nuanced forms of existing measures such as contact maps.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations in other scientific domains.
papers.abstract:
Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for
protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations
present challenges in interpretability. In this work, we demonstrate a set of
methods for analyzing protein Transformer models through the lens of attention.
We show that attention: (1) captures the folding structure of proteins,
connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but
spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites,
a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more
complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We find this
behavior to be consistent across three Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT,
XLNet) and two distinct protein datasets. We also present a three-dimensional
visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Code
for visualization and analysis is available at
https://github.com/salesforce/provis.

papers.title: Emergent effects of scaling on the functional hierarchies within large language models
papers.research_question: What is the functional hierarchy of abstraction across layers in LLMs, and how does it change with model scaling?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit functional hierarchies with abstraction increasing across layers, but scaling introduces deviations such as double representation peaks and anti-persistent fluctuations in attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms functional hierarchies in LLMs but reveals emergent deviations with scaling, such as double representation peaks and layer coordination, complicating interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Item-level semantics are most strongly represented in early layers (2-7), two-item relations in middle layers (8-12), and four-item analogies in later layers (10-15), consistent with an abstraction hierarchy.
Deep layers can represent narrow two-item relations from early in the context, suggesting information compression without meaningful abstraction.
In the large Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct model, representation of two-item relations and analogies shows two distinct peaks (layers 12-16 and 25-33), indicating fluctuations in abstraction level.
Adjacent layers in the large model exhibit anti-persistent fluctuations in attention outputs, with negative autocorrelation, suggesting coordinated specialization.
Buried concepts (target text followed by filler) are represented in deeper layers, showing that late layers capture global document-wide information.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of the double-peak pattern and valley in large models is unclear and requires further work.
Analyses on grammar and syntax were inconclusive and not reported, limiting insights into syntactic processing.
future_direction: Study larger models to understand scaling effects further.
Investigate the mechanisms behind the double-peak representation and layer coordination.
Explore how late-layer representations can be used for steering and safety applications.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) architectures are often described as functionally hierarchical: Early layers process syntax, middle layers begin to parse semantics, and late layers integrate information. The present work revisits these ideas. This research submits simple texts to an LLM (e.g., "A church and organ") and extracts the resulting activations. Then, for each layer, support vector machines and ridge regressions are fit to predict a text's label and thus examine whether a given layer encodes some information. Analyses using a small model (Llama-3.2-3b; 28 layers) partly bolster the common hierarchical perspective: Item-level semantics are most strongly represented early (layers 2-7), then two-item relations (layers 8-12), and then four-item analogies (layers 10-15). Afterward, the representation of items and simple relations gradually decreases in deeper layers that focus on more global information. However, several findings run counter to a steady hierarchy view: First, although deep layers can represent document-wide abstractions, deep layers also compress information from early portions of the context window without meaningful abstraction. Second, when examining a larger model (Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct), stark fluctuations in abstraction level appear: As depth increases, two-item relations and four-item analogies initially increase in their representation, then markedly decrease, and afterward increase again momentarily. This peculiar pattern consistently emerges across several experiments. Third, another emergent effect of scaling is coordination between the attention mechanisms of adjacent layers. Across multiple experiments using the larger model, adjacent layers fluctuate between what information they each specialize in representing. In sum, an abstraction hierarchy often manifests across layers, but large models also deviate from this structure in curious ways.

papers.title: SpectralKD: A Unified Framework for Interpreting and Distilling Vision Transformers via Spectral Analysis
papers.research_question: How can spectral analysis provide a unified framework for interpreting Vision Transformers and optimizing Knowledge Distillation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SpectralKD, a unified framework for interpreting and distilling Vision Transformers via spectral analysis, providing insights into information flow and achieving state-of-the-art knowledge distillation performance without trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: SpectralKD offers a unified framework for interpreting and distilling Vision Transformers, revealing spectral patterns and enabling effective knowledge transfer, opening new research directions in distillation dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Model-wise analysis reveals a U-shaped frequency pattern in CaiT, with early and late layers having higher spectral intensity.
Layer-wise analysis shows early layers have uniform intensity, middle layers decay from low to high frequency, and final layers become uniform again with high intensity.
Swin Transformer and CaiT exhibit similar spectral encoding patterns despite architectural differences.
SpectralKD improves DeiT-Tiny by +5.2% and Swin-Tiny by +1.4% in top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K.
Distilled students reproduce spectral patterns similar to teachers, revealing 'distillation dynamics'.
future_direction: Further exploration of distillation dynamics.
papers.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has achieved widespread success in compressing large Vision Transformers (ViTs), but a unified theoretical framework for both ViTs and KD is still lacking. In this paper, we propose SpectralKD, a novel unified analytical framework that offers deeper insights into ViTs and optimizes KD via spectral analysis. Our model-wise analysis reveals that CaiT concentrates information in their first and last few layers, informing optimal layer selection for KD. Surprisingly, our layer-wise analysis discovers that Swin Transformer and CaiT exhibit similar spectral encoding patterns despite their architectural differences, leading to feature map alignment guideline. Building on these insights, we propose a simple yet effective spectral alignment method for KD. Benefiting from the deeper understanding by above analysis results, even such a simple strategy achieves state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet-1K without introducing any trainable parameters, improving DeiT-Tiny by $+5.2\%$ and Swin-Tiny by $+1.4\%$ in top-1 accuracy. Furthermore, our post-training analysis reveals that distilled students can reproduce spectral patterns similar to their teachers, opening a new area we term ``distillation dynamics". Code and experimental logs are available in https://github.com/thy960112/SpectralKD.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-Correction in LLMs: Towards Explainable Prompting via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does intrinsic self-correction prompting act as representation steering along interpretable latent directions?
papers.core_contribution: Intrinsic self-correction in LLMs functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by alignment between prompt-induced shifts and steering vectors and causal verification via activation addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings link self-correction prompting to representation steering along interpretable latent directions, highlighting the role of interpretability methods in understanding prompt-driven LLM phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Prompt-induced shifts in self-correction align with steering vectors constructed from contrastive pairs.
Activation injection with steering vectors causally reproduces behavioral changes in toxicity.
Detoxification is effective even with weak prompts, while toxification requires strong prompts.
Most of the behavioral change occurs in the first self-correction round.
Alignment between shifts and vectors peaks in mid-to-late layers for some models.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to toxicity-related behaviors and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other prompt-driven phenomena such as chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Intrinsic self-correction refers to the phenomenon where a language model refines its own outputs purely through prompting, without external feedback or parameter updates. While this approach improves performance across diverse tasks, its mechanism remains unclear. We show that intrinsic self-correction functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by both alignment analysis and activation interventions. To achieve this, we analyze intrinsic self-correction via the representation shift induced by prompting. In parallel, we construct interpretable latent directions with contrastive pairs and verify the causal effect of these directions via activation addition. Evaluating six open-source LLMs, our results demonstrate that prompt-induced representation shifts in text detoxification and text toxification consistently align with latent directions constructed from contrastive pairs. In detoxification, the shifts align with the non-toxic direction; in toxification, they align with the toxic direction. These findings suggest that representation steering is the mechanistic driver of intrinsic self-correction. Our analysis highlights that understanding model internals offers a direct route to analyzing the mechanisms of prompt-driven LLM behaviors.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of\n Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the stacked layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interventional, input perturbation-based analysis method to show that Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, with larger contexts and more complex phrase boundaries becoming more salient in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process; structured input perturbations are a useful tool for analyzing deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing characteristic scale of context along layers.
Swapping two constituent phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrase spans of the same length, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, indicating sensitivity to phrase hierarchy.
Changes in attention weights partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance, with deeper layers showing more correlation.
The observed sensitivities are not due to simple co-occurrence statistics, as shown by controlling for PMI.
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features
Searching for the causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance
Exploring applications in network pruning studies
Extending the method as a hypothesis generator in neuroscience to understand compositional structure in neural populations
papers.abstract:
While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models
have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete
accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear
what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations,
nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In
this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of
interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from
pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive
neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of
probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several
kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a
sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the
original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random
permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a
representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which
do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase
structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break
apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure.
 Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build
sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that
hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our
results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of
analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can
serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for
interpreting complex black-box models.

papers.title: Limitations of Normalization in Attention Mechanism
papers.research_question: What are the theoretical and empirical limitations of softmax normalization in attention mechanisms, particularly regarding token separability and gradient sensitivity?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical framework and non-asymptotic bounds that quantify the limitations of softmax normalization in attention mechanisms, specifically regarding token separability and gradient sensitivity, and validates these findings empirically on GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: Softmax attention acts as a capacity-limited selector that discriminates well only when the active token set is a small fraction of the context, and the analysis provides quantitative tools for diagnosing these limits and guidelines for designing more robust normalization strategies.
papers.key_findings:
The representation distance between selected and non-selected tokens collapses when the number of selected tokens N grows proportionally to the context length L, formalizing the 'softmax bottleneck'.
Under spherical embedding assumptions, no more than approximately 80% of the top-N selected tokens can be geometrically distinguished, indicating a hard limit on a single attention head's capacity.
The Jacobian norm of the softmax scales as 1/(4T), creating a trade-off where lower temperature improves token separability but increases gradient sensitivity and training instability.
Empirical experiments on GPT-2 confirm the theoretical predictions of distance collapse, separability saturation, and gradient sensitivity scaling.
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes embeddings are a priori L2-normalized and roughly isotropic, which may not hold in real models.
future_direction: Relaxing the spherical-embedding assumption.
Analyzing multi-query and multi-head interactions.
Designing a single normalization rule that is simultaneously length-adaptive, sparse, and gradient-stable.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the limitations of the normalization in attention mechanisms. We begin with a theoretical framework that enables the identification of the model's selective ability and the geometric separation involved in token selection. Our analysis includes explicit bounds on distances and separation criteria for token vectors under softmax scaling. Through experiments with pre-trained GPT-2 model, we empirically validate our theoretical results and analyze key behaviors of the attention mechanism. Notably, we demonstrate that as the number of selected tokens increases, the model's ability to distinguish informative tokens declines, often converging toward a uniform selection pattern. We also show that gradient sensitivity under softmax normalization presents challenges during training, especially at low temperature settings. These findings advance current understanding of softmax-based attention mechanism and motivate the need for more robust normalization and selection strategies in future attention architectures.

papers.title: Inferring the nature of linguistic computations in the brain
papers.research_question: How can we infer the nature of linguistic computations from neural data, and what are the pitfalls in interpreting such data and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that neural data alone is insufficient to infer the computational mechanisms of sentence processing, and that models must be evaluated based on cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles to be explanatory.
papers.conclusion: Computational modeling is vital for understanding sentence processing, but models must compute linguistically-sufficient representations via explicit cognitive operations and stay faithful to neurophysiological principles, and should not be judged solely on predictive power.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of a 1-2-4 Hz pattern in neural data does not necessarily imply hierarchical processing; it can also arise from associative models.
Artificial neural networks can produce the 1-2-4 Hz pattern without explicit sentence structure, but this does not rule out hierarchical processing in the brain.
Predictive power of a model is not the sole criterion for explaining brain function; models must also be faithful to cognitive and neural principles.
The amount of training data used in ANNs may not reflect the brain's learning environment, and rule-based models might be more explanatory in some cases.
Statistical models are not necessarily more parsimonious than hierarchical models, as they may require extensive training and latent syntactic information.
future_direction: Using naturalistic paradigms to study language processing
Integrating multiple data sources (e.g., EEG, fMRI) to test models
Developing models that are explicit about cognitive operations and neurophysiological implementation
papers.abstract: Sentences contain structure that determines their meaning beyond that of individual words. An influential study by Ding and colleagues (2016) used frequency tagging of phrases and sentences to show that the human brain is sensitive to structure by finding peaks of neural power at the rate at which structures were presented. Since then, there has been a rich debate on how to best explain this pattern of results with profound impact on the language sciences. Models that use hierarchical structure building, as well as models based on associative sequence processing, can predict the neural response, creating an inferential impasse as to which class of models explains the nature of the linguistic computations reflected in the neural readout. In the current manuscript, we discuss pitfalls and common fallacies seen in the conclusions drawn in the literature illustrated by various simulations. We conclude that inferring the neural operations of sentence processing based on these neural data, and any like it, alone, is insufficient. We discuss how to best evaluate models and how to approach the modeling of neural readouts to sentence processing in a manner that remains faithful to cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles.

papers.title: Beyond Components: Singular Vector-Based Interpretability of Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: Can transformer components (attention heads and MLPs) be decomposed into orthogonal singular directions that reveal superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a directional interpretability perspective that decomposes transformer components into orthogonal singular directions, showing that multiple low-rank, interpretable computations coexist within single attention heads and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed, opening new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of learned singular directions can faithfully preserve model behavior.
These directions align with meaningful subfunctions, e.g., in IOI, name mover heads encode multiple overlapping subfunctions along distinct singular directions.
Components identified as part of known circuits exhibit strong engagement along specific singular directions, indicating computations are embedded in compact subspaces.
Transformer computations are distributed, structured, and compositional, with overlapping subfunctions embedded within shared subspaces.
Singular directions can be used for controlled interventions, e.g., in gender pronoun resolution, scaling directions can modify predictions.
papers.limitation: Some directions remain challenging to interpret fully.
future_direction: Conduct targeted intervention experiments to validate causal contributions of discovered components.
Examine whether these mechanisms generalize to larger or more capable models (e.g., Phi, LLaMA).
Explore activation of these mechanisms in real-world settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit complex and distributed behavior, yet their internal computations remain poorly understood. Existing mechanistic interpretability methods typically treat attention heads and multilayer perceptron layers (MLPs) (the building blocks of a transformer architecture) as indivisible units, overlooking possibilities of functional substructure learned within them. In this work, we introduce a more fine-grained perspective that decomposes these components into orthogonal singular directions, revealing superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP. We validate our perspective on widely used standard tasks like Indirect Object Identification (IOI), Gender Pronoun (GP), and Greater Than (GT), showing that previously identified canonical functional heads, such as the name mover, encode multiple overlapping subfunctions aligned with distinct singular directions. Nodes in a computational graph, that are previously identified as circuit elements show strong activation along specific low-rank directions, suggesting that meaningful computations reside in compact subspaces. While some directions remain challenging to interpret fully, our results highlight that transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed. This perspective opens new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability and a deeper understanding of model internals.

papers.title: An Interpretable Neuron Embedding for Static Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How to provide a sample- and class-independent explanation of neurons in a model, and can static knowledge from neuron semantics be used for knowledge distillation without sample-by-sample guidance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to embed neurons into semantic vectors for interpretability, enabling static knowledge distillation that performs comparably to existing methods without sample-by-sample teacher guidance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes neuron embedding for interpretability and static knowledge distillation, demonstrating effective knowledge transfer without instance-specific guidance.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic vectors accurately represent neuron semantics, as shown by similar activation maps for neurons with similar vectors.
The embedding method spontaneously converges to manually annotated semantic vectors without supervision.
Static knowledge distillation achieves performance comparable to or better than existing relation-based knowledge distillation methods.
The method allows for analysis of neuron similar and additive relations.
Without sample-by-sample guidance, SKD is efficient and scalable.
papers.abstract: Although deep neural networks have shown well-performance in various tasks, the poor interpretability of the models is always criticized. In the paper, we propose a new interpretable neural network method, by embedding neurons into the semantic space to extract their intrinsic global semantics. In contrast to previous methods that probe latent knowledge inside the model, the proposed semantic vector externalizes the latent knowledge to static knowledge, which is easy to exploit. Specifically, we assume that neurons with similar activation are of similar semantic information. Afterwards, semantic vectors are optimized by continuously aligning activation similarity and semantic vector similarity during the training of the neural network. The visualization of semantic vectors allows for a qualitative explanation of the neural network. Moreover, we assess the static knowledge quantitatively by knowledge distillation tasks. Empirical experiments of visualization show that semantic vectors describe neuron activation semantics well. Without the sample-by-sample guidance from the teacher model, static knowledge distillation exhibit comparable or even superior performance with existing relation-based knowledge distillation methods.

papers.title: Function Vectors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a compact vector representation of an input-output function (function vector) in transformer language models that can be extracted and used to trigger the task in various contexts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that compact vector representations of input-output functions (function vectors) exist in transformer language models and can be extracted via causal mediation analysis; these vectors robustly trigger the corresponding tasks even in zero-shot and natural text contexts.
papers.conclusion: Function vectors are a compact internal representation of functions in large language models that can be extracted and used to trigger tasks robustly across contexts, and they exhibit compositional properties.
papers.key_findings:
Function vectors can be extracted from a small set of attention heads via causal mediation analysis.
FVs are portable across different contexts, including zero-shot and natural text settings.
FVs often encode the output vocabulary of the task but contain additional information beyond that.
FVs can be composed via vector algebra to create new function vectors for combined tasks.
The causal effect of FVs is strongest when added to middle layers of the network.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to relatively simple functions.
The conditions under which FVs can be composed are not fully characterized.
The extraction method relies on having a set of exemplars for the task.
future_direction: Investigate more complex functions.
Explore the relationship between FVs and other internal representations.
Use FVs for model editing and control.
papers.abstract: We report the presence of a simple neural mechanism that represents an input-output function as a vector within autoregressive transformer language models (LMs). Using causal mediation analysis on a diverse range of in-context-learning (ICL) tasks, we find that a small number attention heads transport a compact representation of the demonstrated task, which we call a function vector (FV). FVs are robust to changes in context, i.e., they trigger execution of the task on inputs such as zero-shot and natural text settings that do not resemble the ICL contexts from which they are collected. We test FVs across a range of tasks, models, and layers and find strong causal effects across settings in middle layers. We investigate the internal structure of FVs and find while that they often contain information that encodes the output space of the function, this information alone is not sufficient to reconstruct an FV. Finally, we test semantic vector composition in FVs, and find that to some extent they can be summed to create vectors that trigger new complex tasks. Our findings show that compact, causal internal vector representations of function abstractions can be explicitly extracted from LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://functions.baulab.info.

papers.title: The Cognitive Revolution in Interpretability: From Explaining Behavior to Interpreting Representations and Algorithms
papers.research_question: How can we understand, interpret, and explain the behavior of complex intelligent AI systems like large language models, and how can mechanistic interpretability be grounded in cognitive science?
papers.core_contribution: The paper grounds mechanistic interpretability in cognitive science, proposing a taxonomy that categorizes interpretation methods into semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a cognitive revolution in deep learning interpretability is underway, shifting from explaining behavior to interpreting representations and algorithms, and calls for a unified framework that integrates semantic and algorithmic interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Current interpretability methods are ripe for a transition echoing the 'cognitive revolution' in psychology, shifting from pure behaviorism to studying internal representations and processing.
A taxonomy mirroring computational neuroscience distinguishes semantic interpretation (studying latent representations) and algorithmic interpretation (studying operations and algorithms).
Semantic interpretation methods include optimization and search, structural probing, causal probing, and dictionary learning, each with distinct assumptions and challenges.
Algorithmic interpretation focuses on circuit discovery, using interventions like knockouts and patching to understand the role of sub-networks in model behavior.
The paper discusses parallels and distinctions between approaches, analyzes strengths and weaknesses, and outlines challenges and the possibility of a unified framework.
future_direction: Unifying semantic and algorithmic interpretation under a common framework.
Addressing challenges in scalability, evaluation, and the Rashomon effect in causal analysis.
Developing automated and scalable methods for feature interpretation and evaluation in dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have long been understood as "black boxes": though we know their computation graphs and learned parameters, the knowledge encoded by these weights and functions they perform are not inherently interpretable. As such, from the early days of deep learning, there have been efforts to explain these models' behavior and understand them internally; and recently, mechanistic interpretability (MI) has emerged as a distinct research area studying the features and implicit algorithms learned by foundation models such as large language models. In this work, we aim to ground MI in the context of cognitive science, which has long struggled with analogous questions in studying and explaining the behavior of "black box" intelligent systems like the human brain. We leverage several important ideas and developments in the history of cognitive science to disentangle divergent objectives in MI and indicate a clear path forward. First, we argue that current methods are ripe to facilitate a transition in deep learning interpretation echoing the "cognitive revolution" in 20th-century psychology that shifted the study of human psychology from pure behaviorism toward mental representations and processing. Second, we propose a taxonomy mirroring key parallels in computational neuroscience to describe two broad categories of MI research, semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned and used) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations) to elucidate their divergent goals and objects of study. Finally, we elaborate the parallels and distinctions between various approaches in both categories, analyze the respective strengths and weaknesses of representative works, clarify underlying assumptions, outline key challenges, and discuss the possibility of unifying these modes of interpretation under a common framework.

papers.title: What Is One Grain of Sand in the Desert? Analyzing Individual Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify and analyze individual neurons in deep NLP models? The paper also investigates how localized or distributed linguistic properties are, whether neurons are exclusive to certain properties, and how information distribution differs between NMT and NLM.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes two methods for identifying and analyzing individual neurons in deep NLP models: a supervised Linguistic Correlation Analysis and an unsupervised Cross-model Correlation Analysis, and demonstrates their effectiveness through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes two methods for extracting salient neurons and demonstrates their accuracy through ablation experiments, with potential applications in model distillation and neural architecture search.
papers.key_findings:
Open class categories (e.g., verb, location) are more distributed across neurons than closed class categories (e.g., coordinating conjunction, determiner).
The model recognizes a hierarchy of linguistic properties and distributes neurons accordingly.
Important neurons extracted from Cross-model Correlation overlap with those from Linguistic Correlation (e.g., position neurons).
Ablating top neurons identified by Cross-model Correlation causes significant performance drop, validating the method.
Using only top neurons, classifiers can regain much of the performance, suggesting potential for model distillation.
future_direction: Applying the methods to model distillation and neural architecture search
Exploring recent architectures like Transformer and QRNN
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable evolution of deep neural networks in natural language processing (NLP), their interpretability remains a challenge. Previous work largely focused on what these models learn at the representation level. We break this analysis down further and study individual dimensions (neurons) in the vector representation learned by end-to-end neural models in NLP tasks. We propose two methods: Linguistic Correlation Analysis, based on a supervised method to extract the most relevant neurons with respect to an extrinsic task, and Cross-model Correlation Analysis, an unsupervised method to extract salient neurons w.r.t. the model itself. We evaluate the effectiveness of our techniques by ablating the identified neurons and reevaluating the network’s performance for two tasks: neural machine translation (NMT) and neural language modeling (NLM).
